questions.text: Which of the following is the most appropriate title for the passage?
questions.context: A defeated army's surrender is often remembered as the moment a war ended, a tidy narrative that obscures how much of the actual outcome was decided weeks or months earlier, once one side's supply lines and troop deployment had already become unsustainable. Military historians who trace a conflict's logistics rather than its battles often find the eventual surrender was less a sudden turning point than a formal acknowledgment of a conclusion that had already become inevitable, simply delayed by a commander unwilling to concede while any option, however costly, still remained technically available.

options.text: Why Surrenders Always Occur Immediately After a Decisive Battle
How Logistics, Not the Final Battle, Often Decides a War's Real Outcome
A History of Formal Surrender Ceremonies
Why Commanders Always Surrender at the Earliest Opportunity
How Military Historians Are Trained to Study Battles

questions.text: Choose the most appropriate topic of the passage.
questions.context: A country experiencing heavy immigration is often assumed by long-term residents to be undergoing an unprecedented cultural shift, an assumption immigration officials rarely allocation resources to correct with historical context. Demographic historians who trace immigration records back several generations routinely find comparable waves in the past, each equally disruptive at the time and each, in due course, absorbed into what residents decades later would describe as simply the country's established culture. The sense of an unprecedented present moment, on this evidence, says less about the actual scale of current immigration than about how selectively short living memory really is.

options.text: the legal process required to obtain permanent residency
how a sense of unprecedented cultural change often reflects the shortness of living memory rather than genuinely unprecedented scale
the economic contributions immigrants make to a host country
why immigration officials rarely publish historical demographic data
a comparison of two specific countries' immigration statistics

questions.text: Choose the most appropriate topic of the passage.
questions.context: A neighbourhood undergoing renewal after a prolonged period of decline is often praised by city officials for its renewed vitality, a framing that can obscure whose vitality is actually being renewed. Long-term residents who could not afford the area during its decline often find themselves unable to afford it during its recovery either, priced out by the very investment their neighbourhood's improvement attracted. Renewal, in this sense, does not simply reverse decline; it can quietly transfer a neighbourhood from one population to another, with the original residents experiencing almost none of the improvement they arguably endured the decline to eventually see.

options.text: the architectural styles typical of neighbourhood renewal projects
how neighbourhood renewal can displace the very residents who endured the preceding decline
the total cost of renovating a declining urban neighbourhood
why city officials rarely announce renewal projects publicly
a comparison of two specific neighbourhoods' renewal outcomes

questions.text: Which of the following best states the main point of the passage?
questions.context: A company's founding culture is often assumed to reproduce itself automatically as the company grows, since new hires are expected to absorb existing norms simply by working alongside longer-serving colleagues. Firms that track this assumption closely find it holds only up to a certain size: beyond a few hundred employees, most new hires no longer work closely enough with founding-era staff to absorb anything by proximity alone, and culture that once transmitted informally must instead be deliberately documented and taught, or it quietly dilutes with each new hiring wave.

options.text: Company culture always reproduces itself automatically regardless of company size.
Beyond a certain size, culture must be deliberately taught rather than absorbed informally.
New hires never absorb any cultural norms from longer-serving colleagues.
Documenting company culture is unnecessary for firms of any size.
Company culture dilutes at exactly the same rate regardless of hiring practices.

questions.text: How many of the statements below do NOT agree with the passage?
questions.context:
I spent years assuming my grandmother's wartime stories were exaggerated, the way I assumed most family stories eventually become exaggerated in the retelling. It wasn't until I found her actual wartime letters, boxed and forgotten in an attic after she passed, that I realised the stories I'd quietly disbelieved for years had, if anything, understated what she'd actually lived through. My mother, reading the same letters, said she'd always suspected there was more to the stories than we'd been told, though she'd never gone looking for proof herself. I now regret every time I let my grandmother's story trail off unfinished because I assumed I already knew where it was going.

Statements
(a) The writer initially assumed her grandmother's wartime stories were exaggerated.
(b) The letters were discovered in an attic after the grandmother had passed away.
(c) The letters revealed the stories had actually exaggerated what really happened.
(d) The mother had previously gone looking for proof behind the stories herself.
(e) The writer now regrets letting some of her grandmother's stories go unfinished.
(f) The mother suspected there was more to the stories than the family had been told.

questions.text: Which statement does NOT agree with the two explanations given in the passage?
questions.context: Military historians studying long-serving veterans who re-enlist repeatedly, despite having satisfied any minimum service requirement long ago, have proposed two competing explanations. One explanation holds that repeated re-enlistment reflects a genuine, deepening commitment to military identity itself, one that grows stronger with each additional tour rather than fading. A second, competing explanation instead proposes that veterans who have spent the bulk of their adult life in service simply lack a comparably developed civilian identity to return to, making re-enlistment less an active choice toward the military than an absence of any equally compelling alternative.

options.text: The first explanation attributes repeated re-enlistment to a deepening commitment to military identity.
The first explanation suggests this commitment grows stronger with each additional tour.
The second explanation claims veterans always possess a fully developed civilian identity to return to.
The second explanation attributes re-enlistment partly to the absence of a compelling civilian alternative.
Both explanations attempt to account for the same pattern of repeated re-enlistment.

questions.text: Which of the following best explains the meaning of the underlined phrase "the founder's halo"?
questions.context: Employees who joined a company during its earliest, most precarious years are often credited, years later, with an almost mythic foresight, a pattern researchers call _the founder's halo_: the same risk tolerance that in hindsight looks like visionary conviction was, at the time, frequently indistinguishable from simply having no better job offer available. The halo forms retroactively, once success has already occurred, and says less about what early employees actually believed at the time than about how success reshapes memory of that belief afterward.

options.text: early employees always genuinely foresaw a company's eventual success in advance
a company's later success can retroactively reshape how early employees' original motivations are remembered
companies that fail never had any early employees with genuine conviction
risk tolerance and lack of alternatives are always clearly distinguishable at the time
memory of a company's founding is always more accurate than memory of its later years

questions.context: A department reorganisation often produces a ① _consequent_ drop in morale during the transition period, even when the reorganisation itself is well designed. Staff asked to ③ _multitask_ across two overlapping structures during the changeover report significantly higher stress than staff moved cleanly from one structure to the other. Leadership teams that clearly ④ _envision_ and communicate the reorganisation's purpose in advance see markedly smoother transitions than those that announce changes without warning. A detailed transition plan, ⑤ _compiled_ hastily the night before announcement, tends to generate more confusion than no plan at all.

confrontation
multitask
envision

questions.text: Which of the following questions CANNOT be answered from the passage?
questions.context: A cargo vessel crossing an ocean carries enough fuel reserve to account for unexpected delays, since running out of fuel mid-ocean with no nearby port poses a far greater risk than simply arriving later than originally scheduled. Shipping companies calculate this reserve based on historical weather patterns along a given route, adding extra fuel for routes with historically higher storm frequency. A vessel that burns through its reserve faster than expected due to an unusually severe storm must radio ahead to arrange refuelling at the nearest available port, a detour that can add days to a voyage but avoids the far costlier alternative of an at-sea rescue.

options.text: Why does a cargo vessel carry a fuel reserve for an ocean crossing?
How do shipping companies calculate the size of this reserve?
How many cargo vessels currently operate on transoceanic routes?
